questions.question: A repair shop serves $N$ machines with $c$ mechanics; each working machine fails at rate $\lambda>0$ independently, repairs take $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ times, and $L(t)$ is the number of machines in repair (waiting or being repaired). Why does the arrival rate of failed machines at the repair shop fall as $L(t)$ increases?
options: Waiting machines see the long repair queue and some decide not to join.
The mechanics work more slowly when many machines are waiting for them.
A machine that is in repair is not running, so it cannot fail again.
The total rate $N\lambda$ is shared among the $L(t)$ machines in repair.

questions.question: A repair shop serves $N$ machines with $c$ mechanics; each working machine fails at rate $\lambda>0$ independently, repairs take $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ times, and $L(t)$ is the number of machines in repair (waiting or being repaired). Why does this model have stationary probabilities $p(n)$ for all values of $\lambda$, $\mu$ and $c\ge1$?
options: $L(t)$ only takes the values $0,\dots,N$, so the normalising sum is finite.
The arrival rate $\lambda(N-n)$ is always below the service rate $\mu c$.
A machine that fails while all mechanics are busy is rejected and lost.
The repair rate $\mu\min\{n,c\}$ grows without bound as $n$ grows.

questions.question: A repair shop serves $N$ machines with $c$ mechanics; each working machine fails at rate $\lambda>0$ independently, repairs take $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ times, and $L(t)$ is the number of machines in repair (waiting or being repaired). When $n\le N-2$ machines are in repair, so that at least two machines are running, why is the time until the next failure exponential with rate $\lambda(N-n)$?
options: The sum of $N-n$ independent $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$ lifetimes.
The maximum of $N-n$ independent $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$ lifetimes.
One $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$ lifetime, scaled by the $N$ machines.
The minimum of $N-n$ independent $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$ lifetimes.

questions.question: A repair shop serves $N$ machines with $c$ mechanics; each working machine fails at rate $\lambda>0$ independently, repairs take $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ times, and $L(t)$ is the number of machines in repair (waiting or being repaired). Assume $N\ge2$. Why can PASTA not be used to say that a failing machine sees the time-average probabilities $p(n)$?
options: Failures are a Poisson process, but the failing machine changes the state it is about to observe.
Failures are not Poisson, since their rate $\lambda(N-n)$ depends on $L(t)$.
PASTA holds only when there are at least as many mechanics as machines.
PASTA holds only for queues with an infinite waiting room and $\lambda<\mu$.

questions.question: A repair shop serves $N$ machines with $c$ mechanics; each working machine fails at rate $\lambda>0$ independently, repairs take $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ times, and $L(t)$ is the number of machines in repair (waiting or being repaired). Let $\pi(n)$ be the long-run fraction of failing machines that find $n$ machines already in repair. What is $\pi(N)$?
options: $\pi(N)=p(N)$, since every machine is equally likely to fail at any time.
$\pi(N)=1-p(0)$, since the failing machine must find the shop busy.
$\pi(N)=0$, since a machine can only fail while it is running.
$\pi(N)=\lambda p(N)/\bar\lambda$, since one machine is left to fail.

questions.question: A factory has $N=5$ machines; each running machine fails at rate $\lambda=0.5$ per week, independently. If $3$ machines are in repair, what is the total rate $\lambda(3)$ at which the next machine fails?
options: $1.5$ per week
$1$ per week
$2.5$ per week
$0.5$ per week

questions.question: A repair shop has $c=2$ mechanics, each repairing at rate $\mu=3$ per day, and $L=5$ machines are in repair (waiting or being repaired). What is the total repair rate $\mu(5)$?
options: $15$ per day
$3$ per day
$9$ per day
$6$ per day

questions.question: A repair shop has $N=4$ machines, $c=1$ mechanic, failure rate $\lambda=1$ per running machine and repair rate $\mu=2$. Using the level-crossing equation between states $0$ and $1$, what is $p(1)/p(0)$?

A repair shop has $N=4$ machines and $c=4$ mechanics, so no machine ever waits; each machine fails at rate $\lambda=1$ and a repair takes $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ with $\mu=3$. What is $\mathbb{E}[L]$, the mean number of machines in repair?

A repair shop has $N=4$ machines that each fail at rate $\lambda=0.5$ per day while running. Its stationary probabilities $p(n)$ give a mean number in repair of $\mathbb{E}[L]=1.2$. What is the long-run failure rate $\bar\lambda$?
options: $2$ per day
$0.6$ per day
$0.8$ per day
$1.4$ per day

questions.question: A repair shop has $N\ge2$ machines that each fail at rate $\lambda>0$ while running and $c=1$ mechanic with $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ repairs. How does the probability $\pi(0)$ that a failing machine finds the mechanic idle compare with the time fraction $p(0)$ that the mechanic is idle?
options: $\pi(0)=p(0)$, because each running machine fails at a constant rate $\lambda$.
$\pi(0)>p(0)$, because failures are most frequent when few machines are down.
$\pi(0)<p(0)$, because a failing machine adds to an already busy shop.
$\pi(0)=p(0)$, because the finite state space makes the model stable.

questions.question: A repair shop serves $N$ machines with $c$ mechanics; each working machine fails at rate $\lambda>0$ independently, repairs take $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ times, and $L(t)$ is the number of machines in repair (waiting or being repaired). Which arrival rate belongs in Little's law $\mathbb{E}[J]=\mathbb{E}[L]/\bar\lambda$ for the mean time $\mathbb{E}[J]$ a machine spends in repair?
options: $\lambda(N-\mathbb{E}[L])$, the long-run rate at which machines fail
$N\lambda$, the failure rate of the factory with all machines running
$\lambda(N-c)$, the failure rate when all mechanics are busy
$\lambda$, the failure rate of a single running machine on its own

questions.question: A repair shop serves $N$ machines with $c$ mechanics; each working machine fails at rate $\lambda>0$ independently, repairs take $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ times, and $L(t)$ is the number of machines in repair (waiting or being repaired). Why may a call centre with a very large number $N$ of potential callers, each calling rarely, be modelled with Poisson arrivals instead?
options: Callers who find a long queue hang up, which makes the arrival rate constant.
For large $N$ the rate $\lambda(N-n)$ becomes zero, so the source plays no role.
Exponential times between calls of one caller already make the total input Poisson.
If $n\ll N$, the rate $\lambda(N-n)$ stays close to the constant $N\lambda$.

questions.question: A repair shop has $N=3$ machines and $c=1$ mechanic, with failure rate $\lambda=1$ per running machine and repair rate $\mu=1$. What is $p(0)$, the long-run fraction of time that all machines are running?

A repair shop has $N=2$ machines and $c=1$ mechanic; each running machine fails at rate $\lambda=\tfrac{1}{2}$ and repairs take $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ with $\mu=1$. The mechanic is idle a fraction $p(0)=0.4$ of the time. Using two expressions for the failure rate $\bar\lambda$, what is $\mathbb{E}[L]$?

A repair shop has $N=2$ machines, $c=1$ mechanic, $\lambda=1$ and $\mu=3$, with stationary probabilities $p=(\tfrac{9}{17},\tfrac{6}{17},\tfrac{2}{17})$ and long-run failure rate $\bar\lambda=\tfrac{24}{17}$. What is the probability that a failing machine finds the mechanic busy?

In a repair shop with $N$ machines, $c$ mechanics and $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ repairs, suppose each machine runs for exactly $1/\lambda$ time units after a repair before failing. Would the birth-death recursion for the probabilities $p(n)$ of $n$ machines in repair still apply, and why?
options: Yes: each machine still fails once per $1/\lambda$ time units on average.
No: the state space would become infinite, so $p(0)$ could not be found.
No: the repair rate would no longer be $\mu\min\{n,c\}$ in state $n$.
No: the number $n$ in repair would not fix when the next failure occurs.

questions.question: A repair shop serves $N$ machines with $c$ mechanics; each working machine fails at rate $\lambda>0$ independently, repairs take $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ times, and $L(t)$ is the number of machines in repair (waiting or being repaired). Let $\rho=\lambda/\mu$. Which statement about the distribution of $L$ when $c=N$ is correct?
options: $L\sim\operatorname{Bin}(N,\rho)$, because $\rho$ is the chance that a given machine is in repair.
$L$ is binomial for every $c\ge1$, since machines fail independently of each other.
Each machine is down a fraction $\rho/(1+\rho)$ of the time, independently, so $L$ is binomial.
$L$ is not binomial, since the failure rate $\lambda(N-n)$ falls as $n$ grows.

questions.question: A repair shop has $N=2$ machines, $c=1$ mechanic and $\lambda=\mu=1$, with stationary probabilities $p=(\tfrac{1}{5},\tfrac{2}{5},\tfrac{2}{5})$. What is the mean time $\mathbb{E}[W]$ that a failed machine waits before its repair starts?

A repair shop has $N=3$ machines and $c=3$ mechanics; each running machine fails at rate $\lambda=2$ and repairs take $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ with $\mu=1$, so $\lambda>\mu$. What is the long-run failure rate $\bar\lambda$?
